brief.prompt: Raw material for a Kubernetes enhancement proposal on in-place pod resource updates. Today Pod.Spec.Containers[i].Resources is immutable, so any change to CPU or memory requests or limits forces the pod to be recreated. Three things drive a change: load rose and the allocation is short; load fell and the allocation sits idle; the values were simply set wrong. Stateless replicas usually survive recreation; low-replica services, stateful workloads and batch jobs pay in availability or cost. Core idea: the spec resources become desired state, and PodStatus is extended to report the resources actually applied. Three CRI gaps also need fixing: UpdateContainerResources takes a Linux-shaped resources parameter that does not fit Windows or future runtimes; there is no CRI call letting kubelet read back the CPU and memory limits a runtime has applied; and the behavior expected of a runtime handling a resource update is not documented. Goals: resize without necessarily restarting the container; let whoever initiated the resize (user, VPA, StatefulSet, JobController) choose what happens when in-place is impossible; let users mark which containers are safe to resize. Non-goals: QoS class change, non-restartable init containers, evicting lower-priority pods to make room, resource types other than CPU and memory, CPU/memory manager policies other than 'None', and resolving scheduler races. Write the motivation and scope section of this KEP for SIG Node reviewers.

brief.prompt: Raw material for a design-details subsection of the in-place pod resize KEP, covering how the kubelet actuates a resize and what happens when a memory limit goes down. The resources the kubelet asks for are not necessarily what the container ends up running with: the Linux kernel enforces minimums on CPU shares and quota, the systemd cgroup driver rounds CPU quota up to the nearest 10ms, and NRI plugins can rewrite the configuration. So a level-triggered comparison of desired against actual cannot decide whether a resize is needed. The kubelet therefore keeps a per-container set of 'actuated' resources: the configuration it handed to the runtime via CreateContainer or UpdateContainerResources and got a success back for. Actuated resources are checkpointed next to allocated resources so they survive a restart; because a badly timed restart can repeat a request, UpdateContainerResources must be idempotent. After a successful CRI resize the pod is marked for resync; if actual does not match desired, that shows up in pod status but is not otherwise acted on. A failed resize is retried on every subsequent pod sync until it succeeds or the container terminates. Lowering a memory limit below current usage: with cgroups v1 the kernel rejects it, with cgroups v2 it triggers an oom-kill. With resize restart policy NotRequired the kubelet reads container memory usage via the StatsProvider and skips the resize for that container when usage exceeds the desired limit; PodResizeInProgress stays with reason Error and a message giving usage and desired limit. This is best-effort: a TOCTOU race remains. The same check runs at pod level before lowering the pod cgroup memory limit. Nodes at v1.33 and earlier check only pod-level usage. Write this design section for kubelet maintainers reviewing the KEP.

brief.prompt: Raw material for the version-skew section of the in-place pod resize KEP. Timeline: the CRI changes merged in v1.25 so runtimes could implement support; containerd added support in 1.6.9. Older clients that do not know the ResizePolicy fields send them as nil, and the API server copies the non-nil values from the old pod forward. The skew problem: before v1.31, with InPlacePodVerticalScaling off, the kubelet read a resource mutation as a change to the container definition and restarted the container with the new values, which can over-subscribe the node. From v1.31 the kubelet no longer treats a resource change as a definition change and does not restart; the new value then takes effect only if the container restarts for some unrelated reason, so the change is nondeterministic and never reflected in the API. Both outcomes are bad, so the API server must reject a resize when the kubelet handling that pod lacks the feature. There is no direct signal, so the proxy is .status.containerStatuses[*].resources, which the kubelet sets on running containers if and only if the feature is enabled; note it is set to an empty {} even when the container declares no requests. Decision logic: feature gate off means reject; otherwise look at the first running container and allow only if its status resources are non-nil; with no running containers, allow. An unscheduled pod may be resized, with the new values used at scheduling and start. A scheduled pod with no running containers gives no signal, so resize is allowed and the node may end up over-provisioned. A race exists where a resize on a non-running container is admitted while the kubelet starts it: before v1.31 the container restarts with the new values, after v1.31 it keeps the old ones. Write the version-skew section for KEP reviewers.

brief.prompt: Raw material for the motivation and scope section of a Kubernetes enhancement proposal on node memory swap support. Two constituencies want swap, and they overlap: node administrators tuning node-level performance and stability and reducing noisy-neighbour effects, and application developers whose programs benefit from swap memory. Three scenarios describe how swap could be used on a node: (1) swap enabled on the host but the kubelet does not let Kubernetes workloads touch it; (2) swap enabled at node level, with the kubelet permitting workloads scheduled there to use some configured quantity; (3) swap set per workload, with the kubelet setting a limit for each one. Scenario 1 is a prerequisite for the rest. This proposal covers 1 and 2 only; 3 goes to a follow-up KEP, and the enablement work here is what that follow-up needs. Goals: on Linux, kubelet can start when swap is provisioned and available; a configuration knob sets how much swap is available to workloads, defaulting to zero; cluster administrators configure this per node; swap works with cgroups v2. Non-goals: non-Linux operating systems, provisioning the swap itself, setting swappiness (already settable system-wide), per-workload allocation with accounting or APIs for customizing how limits are computed (so swap is an overcommitted resource here), zram, zswap, SGX EPC, cgroups v1, pod-level swap API, scheduling that targets swap-enabled nodes, and making the eviction manager swap-aware — the existing QoS-tier eviction hierarchy is kept as is. Write the motivation, scenarios, goals and non-goals section of this KEP for SIG Node reviewers.

brief.prompt: Raw material for the section of the node-swap KEP that specifies how a container's swap limit is computed. Swap access is granted only to Burstable QoS pods, and the values are computed automatically rather than entered by the user. Two steps. First, take the container's memory request divided by the node's total physical memory; call that ContainerMemoryProportion. If a container has memory requests equal to memory limits, its proportion is defined as zero, so its swap limit works out to zero. Second, multiply that proportion by TotalPodsSwapAvailable, which is the total swap on the system minus the system-reserved memory — the residue that keeps swap available to system-critical daemons, since the kernel has no memory.swap.min to reserve with. Worked example: a Burstable pod with container A requesting 20 GB and container B requesting 10 GB, on a node with 40 GB of physical memory and 40 GB of swap, with system-reserved memory configured at 2 GB. Proportions come out at 0.5 and 0.25; TotalPodsSwapAvailable is 38 GB; A gets a 19 GB swap limit and B gets 9.5 GB. The scheme ties each container's share of swap to its memory request and rescales it against whatever swap the system actually has. Write this calculation section of the KEP for reviewers who will implement and test it.

brief.prompt: Raw material for the risks section of the node-swap KEP, covering four risks and what was done about each. Resource exhaustion: earlier releases offered an UnlimitedSwap option for workloads, which let a workload consume all the swap on a node and push the node unhealthy; UnlimitedSwap was dropped from the API in beta2. Security: swap on an unencrypted disk can put critical information, including Kubernetes secrets, onto disk where anyone with disk access can read it; the mitigation is encrypted swap, but handling encryption is a general OS configuration concern outside the kubelet's remit, so the answer is documentation that warns users. Cgroups v1: supporting it was an early goal, but sig-node concluded that swap on cgroup v1 would be very difficult, so the feature is limited to cgroups v2; cgroup v1 is expected to be deprecated eventually, which blunts the inconvenience. Memory-backed volumes: Kubernetes guarantees some volumes never reside on disk — secrets, memory-backed emptyDirs — and the kubelet mounts them as tmpfs on the host. When --fail-swap-on=false, the tmpfs noswap option is used to keep those pages off disk. That option needs kernel 6.4 or newer, though distributions may backport it, so the kubelet uses it when the kernel is at least 6.4, otherwise tries mounting a dummy volume with noswap to detect a backport, and otherwise warns that the option is unsupported. Once support is widespread this probe can go away. Write this risks-and-mitigations section for KEP reviewers.

brief.prompt: Raw material for the motivation and goals section of a Kubernetes enhancement proposal on pod scheduling readiness. Today a pod is treated as ready for scheduling the moment it is created, and the scheduler keeps trying to place every pending pod. In practice some pods sit for long stretches missing an essential resource, and the repeated attempts churn the scheduler and the downstream integrators that watch it, such as Cluster Autoscaler. Without a way to flag a pod as paused, those cycles are spent retrying pods already known to be unschedulable, which delays other pods and lowers overall scheduling throughput; it also constrains vendors who want to build features such as hierarchical quota natively. A constraint on any solution: the condition {type:PodScheduled, reason:Unschedulable} is the canonical signal the scheduler publishes so integrators such as Cluster Autoscaler know to add cluster resources, and that contract must not break. What the proposal wants: an API to mark pods scheduling-paused or scheduling-ready; a new Enqueue extension point so queueing behavior can be customized; paused pods must not be marked Unschedulable through the PodScheduled condition; and a default enqueue plugin that honors the new API's semantics. Out of scope: forcing pod conditions to expose more context about paused pods, and focusing on in-house uses of the Enqueue extension point. Noted as future work: permission control on individual scheduling gates, which depends on a fine-grained permissions design. Write the motivation, goals and non-goals section of this KEP for SIG Scheduling reviewers.

brief.prompt: Raw material for the constraints-and-caveats section of the pod scheduling readiness KEP, about the new .spec.schedulingGates field. State transitions are deliberately restricted. The field can only be initialized when the pod is created, either by the client or by a mutating admission webhook. After creation, gates may be removed in any order, but adding a new gate is not allowed. A scheduled pod must always carry empty scheduling gates, which means a client — administrator or custom controller — cannot create a pod that has schedulingGates populated and also specifies spec.nodeName; the API server returns a validation error. Stated as a matrix: for an unscheduled pod with nil nodeName, create with non-nil gates is allowed and update is not, while nil gates allow both; for a scheduled pod with non-nil nodeName, neither create nor update with non-nil gates is allowed, and nil gates allow both. Feature-gating is not uniform across the three parts of the feature: (a) the pod spec field plus feature gate and associated bits, (b) the SchedulingGates scheduler plugin, and (c) the underlying scheduler framework change, the new PreEnqueue extension point. Disabling the feature turns off a and b but leaves c on, so a plugin developer can use c alone to build their own equivalents of a and b. Separately, kubectl gets a new phase literal, SchedulingPaused, in the phase column of kubectl get pod, to show whether a pod is scheduling-paused. Write this notes and constraints section of the KEP for API and scheduler reviewers.
